statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music played during a psychedelic session changes how it goes or what follows: no study read here compared sessions with and without music, or with different music. In an open-label trial of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (Kaelen et al., 2018), 19 patients each had two psilocybin sessions lying with eye-shades in a furnished room in a clinical research facility, with two therapists and one standard playlist (one patient who strongly disliked it in the first session heard a different playlist in the second). In interviews a week after the second session, 18 of 19 described welcome influences of the music (it intensified the experience for 17, guided 15 and calmed 10) and 10 of 19 unwelcome ones (it intensified feelings they did not want, or felt uncomfortable or irritating); 9 resisted where the music was taking them and 6 felt misguided by it, mostly by music that clashed with what they were going through. Four researchers' ratings of how much each patient had liked the music, resonated with it and been open to it, made from those interviews, correlated with the fall in self-rated depression recorded at the same time point, a week after the second session (liking r = 0.60, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.83; resonance 0.59, 0.19 to 0.82; openness 0.57, 0.16 to 0.81; editors' intervals), while the patients' own rating of how intense the drug had been did not (r = 0.004, −0.45 to 0.46). The music was rated after any improvement had happened, at the same time point, so patients who felt better may have described it more warmly; the three ratings were so closely related (r 0.90 to 0.96) that they probably measure one thing, agreement between the raters averaged r = 0.6 (the authors call this good), nothing was adjusted, and the authors say that without a placebo condition causal inferences are problematic. In a US online panel of 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, 30 (4.9%) named disagreeable music among the things associated with their most challenging experience; naming it was not associated with how challenging they rated the experience (standardized beta 0.05, p = 0.19) nor, with an interval too wide to tell, with thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21, with the other listed factors entered together), and 99 (16.2%) ticked changing the music among actions that had helped during it (Simonsson et al., 2023). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study of 19 patients given psilocybin in a clinic, almost all said the music helped at times, and about half said it sometimes made things harder. Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression, but both were measured at the same time, a week later, so feeling better may have coloured how they described the music. None of the studies we read compared sessions with and without music.
population: Patients with treatment-resistant depression in an open-label psilocybin trial (19), and US adults who had used classic psychedelics in an online panel (613)
exposure: Music played during psilocybin sessions (one standard playlist, with one exception), as patients described it a week later; disagreeable music named as associated with a most challenging experience
comparator: None for music itself: every patient heard music; patients who described it less favourably, and panel respondents who did not name the music
outcome: What patients said the music did; fall in self-rated depression (QIDS) one week after; challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire); thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others in the days or weeks after
magnitude: Kaelen et al. (2018), n = 19: welcome influences 18 of 19, unwelcome 10 of 19; QIDS fall with music liking r = 0.60 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.83, editors'), resonance 0.59, openness 0.57; drug intensity r = 0.004 (−0.45 to 0.46). Simonsson et al. (2023): disagreeable music named by 30 of 613, not associated with challenge (beta 0.05, p = 0.19) or, imprecisely, with later thoughts or attempts of harm (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21); changing the music ticked as helpful by 99 of 613.

risk_of_bias.note: The music experience was rated from interviews at the same visit as the outcome and a week after the sessions, with no adjustment, no music-free condition and predictors chosen from the same transcripts (card sc_kaelen_2018, overall very high); the panel survey's attributions are retrospective (sc_simonsson_2023).

inconsistency.note: The two sources answer different questions.

indirectness.note: Worded for patients in a hospital trial and a US panel.

imprecision.note: 19 patients; the interval for the main correlation runs from 0.20 to 0.83; the panel's harm estimate for music rests on 30 people (interval 0.87 to 8.21).

grade.reasoning: Correlational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one for imprecision, giving very low (the floor). Status single study: the music-outcome association rests on one small trial; the panel survey adds only null associations, one of them very imprecise, for music named as associated with a difficult experience. A 2025 opinion article argues against music in therapy settings and notes that no controlled study compares music with silence; it has no card in this round. A randomized comparison of musical genres in psilocybin sessions (Strickland et al., 2021) is on the project's list and has not yet been read; by its title it compares genres, not music with silence.
